title: WA premier lobbied Albanese to kill Greens deal on environmental reform in eleventh hour intervention
text:

中文新闻

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

TOK PISIN

Topic:Environmental Policy

Tanya Plibersek's signature environmental reforms appear unlikely to pass. (AAP: Lukas Coch)

There will be no deal with the Greens to pass cornerstone environmental protection laws this year amid concerns inside Labor of a backlash from WA.

WA Premier Roger Cook said he lobbied the government to put forward his view that the laws should not proceed.

The government is still pushing for Greens support to pass separate Future Made in Australia legislation to offer tax incentives for hydrogen and critical minerals producers.

Anthony Albanese personally promised WA Premier Roger Cook that the federal government would shelve cornerstone environmental reforms, a sign of the state's critical importance to Labor maintaining a majority.

Mr Cook indicated he spoke to Mr Albanese on Tuesday during an intense day of last-minute crossbench negotiations between Environment Minister Tanya Plibersek and Greens counterpart Sarah-Hanson Young on a deal that was said to have "come close" to success.

"I reiterated the West Australian government's point of view about the Nature Positive laws in their current form should not be progressed," Mr Cook said.

He added that he is "very pleased to receive assurances" that the reforms have been put on ice.

"That gives us a good opportunity to continue to work with industry in relation to how we can continue to resolve any difficulties to… ensure we make environmental stewardship one of our key objectives."

Mr Cook's intervention, which he characterised as being reflective of a "unity WA ticket" with the state's business and mining industry, leaves Mr Albanese vulnerable to Greens' accusations that he has capitulated to the demands of resources companies over environmentalists' concerns.

"I won't comment in relation to the goings-on in Canberra, I simply made sure that Western Australia's view was put forward and put forward effectively," Mr Cook said.

"I believe that position has prevailed."

It is understood Mr Albanese took the decision to scrap efforts to cut a deal with the Greens after that conversation, even as talks were ongoing between Ms Plibersek and Senator Hanson-Young.

There will be "no deal this week", a senior government source told the ABC earlier on Wednesday.

Senator Sarah Hanson-Young last week revived prospects of an agreement to overhaul the Environmental Protection and Biodiversity Act after she offered to drop demands for a "climate trigger" in return for greater protections against native forest logging.

Since then, the two sides have held a series of talks in which they sought to hash out an agreement that would have established an independent environmental "cop" and helped streamline project approvals.

Intense negotiations between Sarah Hanson-Young and Tanya Plibersek were unable to break a deadlock on environmental reforms. (
               ABC News: Matt Roberts
            )

The changes were at the centre of Labor's 2022 election environmental platform and originally had the backing of the Business Council of Australia and environmental groups.

However, demands by Greens leader Adam Bandt and environmental groups that the legislation include rules that would force regulators to assess the climate impact of resource projects left the changes in limbo for most of the past year and fuelled resistance from resource groups.

While talks resumed earlier this month, failure to pass the legislation this week comes close to effectively scuttling the changes amid widespread speculation the government may not return to parliament ahead of an election next year. At present, parliament is due to return in February.

Shelving the so-called Nature Positive reforms follows the government's decision to halt efforts to legislate a ban on gambling advertising.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is understood to be reluctant to countenance further deal-making with the crossbench, with Labor sensing the Greens are losing votes for holding out on key legislation.

The proposed environmental changes also spooked Labor about its election prospects in WA, where mining groups are staunchly opposed.

"This is dangerous territory that the federal government is entering, doing deals in the twilight of the parliamentary term," Warren Pearce, chief executive of the Perth-based Association of Mining and Exploration Companies, warned on Tuesday.

"This legislation is flawed and has been from day dot.

"It is a shame that the government has done more consultation with the crossbench than it has with industry."

Warren Pearce opposed the reforms. (ABC News: West Matteeussen)

The prime minister's decision to dump the Nature Positive reforms comes amid a renewed focus on "bread and butter priorities".

The end-of-year legislative rush means Labor has chosen to elevate the importance of its social media changes, the Future Made in Australia reforms, and immigration changes.

A spokesperson for Ms Plibersek indicated the Greens could still pass Labor's legislation as it currently stands without including Senator Hanson-Young's insistence on toughening up protections for native forests.

"The bills are listed in the Senate. The Coalition, the Greens and other senators can support them at any time," she said.

Senator Hanson-Young said it was the government who had backed off a deal.

"The Greens put a deal on the table, and the government has walked away," she said.

"The prime minister has been bullied by the mining and logging lobby again.

"Gina Rinehart and the logging lobby seem to have more influence than the rest of the country.

"The Greens want to get laws that would actually provide some protection for nature, but Labor couldn't even entertain protecting forests and critical habitat in an extinction crisis."

Felicity Wade, co-convener of the Labor Environmental Action Network, which works within the party for conservation outcomes, declared "today is a hard day for true believers".

"Vested interests won," she said.

"The EPA was an election commitment. It has been in the national platform since 2018 and is backed by 500 local ALP branches. It is core to our claim of caring about the natural environment.

"The minister had stared down the Greens. The deal on the table avoided all the contentious stuff, it was sensible regulatory reform. All of it was existing government policy.

"Environment standards, the key to the deal, were recommended by Graeme Samuel and by the government's own Senate committee. The current act fails because its all process, no outcomes. The standards allow the establishment of decision-making rules that provide the certainty business says it needs.

"This was a chance to show strength and conviction. We know these are things the electorate are looking for from us. And we faltered.

"In the process we leave a completely broken system in place that is stymieing economic activity with its inefficiencies, while also maintaining our place as the extinction capital of the world.

"The renewable energy sector identify the current environment laws with their inconsistencies and glacial pace of approvals as the most material risk to delivery of the government's 82 per cent renewables goal.

"Rio Tinto has come out calling for the passing of these bills because it too needs standards to make rational choices about investment. But the barbarians flexed their muscles and that was that."
